We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}4\cdot {6}^{x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}4\cdot {6}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{{6}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[{6}^{x}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }({6}^{0}-{6}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\cdot (1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{6}^{a})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y={6}^{x}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{6}^{x}=0$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{6}^{x}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14042659/assets/2ebee84cf543b25e56b360f145459696554a3b67daaf64c21812cb4b92fa420a.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}4\cdot {6}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\cdot (1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{6}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\cdot (1-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}.\end{aligned}
$$
